overview: The incident response lifecycle is the structured, repeatable process a data engineering team follows when a data product breaks: it moves from detecting a problem, to triaging its severity and blast radius, to mitigating the impact quickly, to resolving the root cause permanently.

In data engineering the 'incident' is rarely a server being down; it is more often stale data, a bad load, a schema change, a null spike, or a broken transformation that silently poisons dashboards, SLAs, and ML features while every job still shows green.

The lifecycle exists to make chaotic firefighting predictable: clear roles (incident commander, comms lead, scribe), clear severity levels, clear communication cadence, and a clean handoff to a blameless postmortem, all measured with MTTD, MTTA, MTTR, and MTTU so the team improves over time.
learningObjectives: Explain the four phases of the incident response lifecycle (detect, triage, mitigate, resolve) as they apply specifically to data pipelines and data products.
Distinguish mitigation (restore trusted data fast) from resolution (fix the root cause permanently) and know why they are separate steps.
Assign severity, compute blast radius via lineage, run an incident bridge with defined roles, and measure the process with MTTD, MTTA, MTTR, and MTTU.
Apply concrete tooling (Airflow, dbt, Spark, Kafka, Snowflake/BigQuery, Prometheus/Grafana, PagerDuty, Great Expectations, OpenLineage) to each phase and hand off cleanly to a blameless postmortem.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: The incident response lifecycle is a defined operational process for managing data-reliability incidents through four sequential-but-overlapping phases: detection (automated or human recognition that a data SLI or SLA is breached), triage (assessing severity, quantifying blast radius via lineage, and formally declaring an incident with assigned roles), mitigation (short-term actions that stop the bleeding and restore trusted data or service to consumers), and resolution (root-cause remediation, reprocessing/backfill, verification that SLIs have recovered, and closure with a handoff to a blameless postmortem), all measured by lifecycle metrics such as MTTD, MTTA, MTTR, and MTTU.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Think of a data pipeline like a water supply for a city. First a sensor notices the water is contaminated (detect). Then someone checks how bad it is and which neighborhoods are affected, and calls the emergency team together with clear jobs (triage). The team shuts the contaminated valve and switches everyone to reservoir water so people still have something safe to drink right now (mitigate). Finally, engineers find and fix the leak in the pipe, flush the whole system, confirm the water is clean again, and write down what happened so it does not recur (resolve). Restoring safe water fast is mitigation; fixing the pipe for good is resolution.
coreConcept.historicalContext: Incident response as a formal discipline grew out of IT service management (ITIL in the late 1980s/1990s) and matured with Google's Site Reliability Engineering practices published in the 2016 SRE Book, which codified severity levels, the incident commander model (borrowed from the US Incident Command System used by fire services), error budgets, and blameless postmortems. For years these ideas were applied only to online services. As data became a product with its own SLAs, the data observability movement (Monte Carlo, Bigeye, ~2019) and lineage standards like OpenLineage (2020) adapted incident response to data: freshness and volume anomalies replaced HTTP 500s, blast radius is computed through column-level lineage instead of service dependency graphs, and mitigation means serving last-known-good data rather than failing over a web server. Modern data platforms now run on-call rotations, PagerDuty schedules, and incident bridges just like application SRE teams.

whyItMatters.business: A bad data load feeding an executive revenue dashboard or a pricing model can drive wrong decisions worth millions, trigger failed regulatory filings, or erode stakeholder trust; a fast, structured lifecycle limits how long bad data is consumed and how many decisions it corrupts.
whyItMatters.engineering: A defined lifecycle converts panicked, hero-driven firefighting into a repeatable process with clear roles and communication, which shortens outages, reduces cognitive load during stress, and produces postmortems that make the next incident less likely.
whyItMatters.scalability: As the number of pipelines, sources, and downstream consumers grows into the hundreds, ad-hoc response does not scale; standardized severity, on-call rotation, and lineage-driven triage let a small platform team manage reliability across a large data estate.
whyItMatters.cost: Every hour of 'data downtime' has a cost in wasted compute reprocessing, engineer time, and bad business outcomes; reducing MTTD and MTTR directly reduces that cost, and mitigation-first thinking avoids expensive full backfills when serving last-known-good is enough.
whyItMatters.reliability: Treating data products with SLOs and an incident lifecycle makes reliability measurable and enforceable, so consumers know exactly what freshness and correctness guarantees they get and the team knows when they are burning their error budget.

coreComponents.name: Detection Layer (SLIs and Alerting)
coreComponents.definition: The automated and human mechanisms that recognize a data incident is occurring, based on service level indicators like freshness, volume, null rate, distribution, and schema.
coreComponents.purpose: To minimize MTTD (mean time to detect) by catching a broken data product before a downstream consumer does.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Compute SLIs continuously, compare against baselines/thresholds, fire alerts to the right on-call, and provide enough context (which table, which check, which metric) to start triage.
coreComponents.examples: A Great Expectations checkpoint failing on null spike, a Prometheus freshness rule firing when a Snowflake table hasn't updated by 6 AM, a Monte Carlo volume anomaly, an Airflow DAG SLA miss paging PagerDuty.

coreComponents.name: Triage and Roles
coreComponents.definition: The assessment step that assigns a severity, quantifies blast radius via lineage, and formally declares an incident with named roles.
coreComponents.purpose: To right-size the response, pull in the right people, and establish command so the mitigation is coordinated rather than chaotic.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Assign severity (SEV1-SEV4), identify affected downstream tables/dashboards/models via OpenLineage, appoint an incident commander, comms lead, and scribe, and open the incident channel/bridge.
coreComponents.examples: Declaring SEV1 because a bad load hit the finance mart feeding the board deck, using column-level lineage to find 42 impacted downstream dbt models, spinning up a #inc-2026-0142 Slack channel via an incident bot.

coreComponents.name: Mitigation Actions
coreComponents.definition: Short-term interventions that stop the bleeding and restore trustworthy data or service to consumers, without necessarily fixing the underlying cause.
coreComponents.purpose: To reduce customer/consumer impact fast, decoupling recovery of service from the slower root-cause fix.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Pause the offending DAG, quarantine the bad partition, roll back a dbt model to a previous version, serve last-known-good data, and communicate status to consumers.
coreComponents.examples: Pausing an Airflow DAG, swapping a Snowflake view to point at yesterday's good snapshot, reverting a dbt model to the last passing Git SHA, posting a banner on the dashboard warning of degraded data.

coreComponents.name: Resolution and Recovery
coreComponents.definition: The permanent fix: root-cause remediation, reprocessing or backfilling the affected data, verifying SLIs have recovered, and closing the incident.
coreComponents.purpose: To ensure the same failure does not recur and that the data is fully correct again, not just temporarily patched.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Deploy the code/config fix, backfill impacted partitions, re-run downstream models, verify quality checks pass and freshness caught up, and formally close with a postmortem handoff.
coreComponents.examples: Fixing a source schema mapping in dbt, running a partition-scoped Spark/dbt backfill, confirming the finance mart reconciles to source, closing #inc-2026-0142 and scheduling the postmortem.

coreComponents.name: Communication and Command Structure
coreComponents.definition: The roles, cadence, and channels that keep the response coordinated and stakeholders informed throughout the lifecycle.
coreComponents.purpose: To prevent duplicated effort, keep decision-making clear, and manage stakeholder expectations during data downtime.
coreComponents.responsibilities: The incident commander owns decisions, the comms lead updates stakeholders on a fixed cadence, the scribe keeps a timeline, and a bridge/war room centralizes coordination.
coreComponents.examples: An incident commander running a Zoom bridge, a comms lead posting a stakeholder update every 30 minutes for a SEV1, a scribe logging each action with timestamps for the postmortem timeline.

internalWorking: Detection: SLIs (freshness lag, row-count delta, null rate, distribution drift, schema hash) are computed on every load and compared against baselines; a breach fires an alert through Alertmanager/PagerDuty to the on-call, timestamped as the detection moment (drives MTTD).

Acknowledgement and triage: the on-call acks the page (MTTA), then assesses severity using impact (which consumers) and scope (how many datasets); blast radius is computed by traversing OpenLineage from the broken table to all downstream models, dashboards, and features.

Declaration: if severity warrants, the on-call declares an incident, an incident bot opens a dedicated channel and bridge, and roles are assigned (incident commander, comms lead, scribe); a status page/stakeholder message goes out.

Mitigation: the team executes the fastest safe action to restore trust, for example pausing the DAG so no more bad data lands, quarantining the bad partition, rolling back the dbt model, or repointing consumers at last-known-good; this stops impact growing while the true fix is worked (drives MTTR for service restoration).

Resolution: engineers diagnose and deploy the root-cause fix, then reprocess/backfill the affected partitions and re-run downstream models; SLIs are re-checked to confirm recovery (freshness caught up, quality checks green, reconciliation matches source) (drives MTTU, time to full resolution).

Closure and learning: once SLIs are verified healthy, the incident commander declares resolution, closes the channel, and hands off a timeline to a blameless postmortem where contributing factors and action items are captured.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: Data source -> Ingest (Kafka/Airflow) -> Transform (dbt/Spark) -> Warehouse (Snowflake/BigQuery) -> SLI checks (Great Expectations) -> Detect: anomaly/freshness/quality alert -> Alertmanager -> PagerDuty page on-call -> Triage: severity + lineage blast radius (OpenLineage) -> Declare incident -> Incident bot opens channel + roles (IC/comms/scribe) -> Mitigate: pause DAG | quarantine partition | rollback dbt model | serve last-known-good -> Communicate to consumers -> Resolve: root-cause fix -> backfill/reprocess -> verify SLIs recovered -> Close incident -> Blameless postmortem + action items
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. At 05:50 a Kafka-fed Airflow DAG loads the daily orders partition into Snowflake; an upstream API change silently starts sending amount in cents instead of dollars, so a dbt model produces revenue 100x too high.

2. At 06:05 a Great Expectations check on the revenue mart flags a distribution anomaly and a Prometheus freshness/volume rule stays green (data arrived, it is just wrong); the GE failure pages the data on-call via PagerDuty. MTTD is 15 minutes.

3. The on-call acks at 06:12 (MTTA 7 minutes), queries OpenLineage, and finds the bad model feeds the executive revenue dashboard plus 11 downstream dbt models and a pricing feature table; severity is set to SEV1 because the board deck is due at 08:00.
4. An incident is declared: #inc-2026-0142 opens, an incident commander, comms lead, and scribe are named, and a stakeholder message announces degraded revenue data.

5. Mitigation: the team pauses the orders DAG, repoints the dashboard view to yesterday's validated snapshot (last-known-good), and quarantines today's partition. Consumers see clearly-labeled stale-but-correct data instead of wrong data. Service is restored at 06:40 (MTTR ~35 minutes).

6. Resolution: engineers patch the dbt model to divide the miscoded field by 100 (and add a validity check), backfill the quarantined partition, re-run the 11 downstream models, and confirm the mart reconciles to source and all SLIs are green. The incident is closed at 07:30 (MTTU ~85 minutes) and a blameless postmortem is scheduled.

keyTerminology.meaning: A classification (commonly SEV1 to SEV4/5) of how serious an incident is, based on consumer impact and scope.
keyTerminology.importance: Severity right-sizes the response, sets the communication cadence, and determines who gets paged and how urgently.

keyTerminology.meaning: The full set of downstream datasets, dashboards, models, and consumers affected by a data incident, discovered via lineage.
keyTerminology.importance: It determines true severity and which consumers must be warned; a small-looking table can feed dozens of critical products.

keyTerminology.meaning: The single person who owns coordination and decision-making for the incident (not necessarily the one fixing it).
keyTerminology.importance: Clear command prevents chaos and duplicated effort and ensures someone is accountable for driving to resolution.

keyTerminology.meaning: Mean Time To Detect (issue to alert), Acknowledge (alert to human ack), Restore/Mitigate (issue to service restored), and (Ultimate) Resolve (issue to permanent fix).
keyTerminology.importance: These metrics quantify how well the lifecycle works and reveal whether to invest in detection, on-call, or remediation tooling.

keyTerminology.meaning: Mitigation is a fast action that restores trusted service; resolution is the permanent root-cause fix and full data recovery.
keyTerminology.importance: Confusing them causes teams to spend an outage chasing root cause while consumers keep getting bad data.

keyTerminology.meaning: The most recent validated snapshot of a dataset that can be served to consumers while the current bad data is fixed.
keyTerminology.importance: Serving LKG is a core data-specific mitigation that keeps consumers safe without waiting for a full fix.

keyTerminology.meaning: A structured, no-blame review after an incident documenting the timeline, contributing factors, and action items.
keyTerminology.importance: It turns each incident into systemic improvement and psychological safety, encouraging honest disclosure of contributing factors.

keyTerminology.meaning: The synchronous coordination space (call plus dedicated Slack channel) where the response team works the incident together.
keyTerminology.importance: Centralizing communication avoids fragmented side-conversations and keeps everyone on the same shared context.

importantConcepts.explanation: What: the first goal is to stop consumers being harmed, not to find the root cause. Why: root-cause analysis can take hours while bad data keeps flowing every minute. How: pause the DAG, quarantine the partition, or serve last-known-good first, then investigate calmly. Pitfall: engineers who dive straight into debugging leave wrong data live in dashboards for the entire investigation.

importantConcepts.concept: Green jobs can still be incidents
importantConcepts.explanation: What: in data engineering the pipeline can run successfully while the data is wrong, so detection must monitor data content, not just job status. Why: orchestrators report whether code ran, not whether the output is correct. How: layer freshness, volume, and quality SLIs on top of job monitoring. Pitfall: teams that only page on task failures never detect silent corruption until a stakeholder complains.

What: blast radius and true severity come from knowing what depends on the broken table. Why: impact, not the table itself, sets severity. How: query OpenLineage / dbt's DAG / warehouse dependency graph to enumerate downstream consumers. Pitfall: without lineage, teams either overreact to trivial issues or underreact to a small table feeding the board deck.

What: a coordinated response with an incident commander, comms lead, and scribe outperforms a lone hero. Why: one person cannot fix, communicate, and document simultaneously under stress. How: assign roles at declaration time. Pitfall: without a comms lead, stakeholders spam responders for updates and slow the fix; without a scribe, the postmortem timeline is lost.

variationsAndTypes: **Severity levels:** SEV1 (critical, board/customer-facing data wrong, full response), SEV2 (major, important product degraded), SEV3 (minor, contained or non-critical), SEV4 (low, cosmetic or informational).
**Preventive vs reactive detection:** quality gates that block a bad load before publish versus observability/anomaly monitors that alert after data lands.
**Mitigation styles:** stop-the-source (pause DAG), isolate (quarantine partition), roll back (revert dbt model/version), and serve-around (last-known-good snapshot).
**Resolution styles:** forward fix (patch code and reprocess forward), full backfill (reprocess all affected partitions), and reconciliation (delete-insert or MERGE to correct in place).
**On-call models:** follow-the-sun rotations across regions versus a single primary/secondary rotation, both managed in PagerDuty/Opsgenie schedules.
**Automated vs manual response:** self-healing runbooks (auto-pause DAG on quality failure) versus human-driven bridges for ambiguous incidents.
advantages: **Bounded impact:** a structured lifecycle limits how long and how widely bad data is consumed by mitigating fast and communicating clearly.
**Predictable under stress:** defined roles and severity remove ambiguity during high-pressure incidents so responders act instead of deliberating.
**Measurable improvement:** MTTD/MTTA/MTTR/MTTU turn reliability into trackable metrics that justify tooling investment.
**Faster recovery:** separating mitigation from resolution restores trusted data to consumers quickly without waiting for the permanent fix.
**Organizational learning:** blameless postmortems convert incidents into systemic fixes, steadily reducing recurrence.
disadvantages: **Process overhead:** formal declaration, roles, and cadence can feel heavy for genuinely small issues if severity is not tiered.
**Requires investment:** effective detection and triage depend on observability, lineage, and on-call tooling that must be built and maintained.
**Alert fatigue risk:** poorly tuned SLIs page the on-call constantly and desensitize the team, delaying real detection.
**Lineage gaps:** if lineage is incomplete, triage under-scopes blast radius and consumers get missed.
**On-call burden:** rotations and after-hours pages create real human cost and burnout if incident volume is not managed.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use the full lifecycle for data products with real consumers and SLAs (executive dashboards, customer-facing metrics, ML features, regulatory reports) where wrong or stale data causes measurable harm, and staff an on-call rotation for anything mission-critical.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Do not invoke heavyweight incident process for transient dev tables, one-off exploratory analyses, or low-stakes internal datasets; a lightweight ticket and self-service fix is enough, and reserving formal SEVs for real impact avoids process fatigue.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: The lifecycle mirrors a hospital emergency room. Triage nurses assess how urgent each patient is (severity and blast radius). A trauma lead coordinates the team while a nurse charts everything (incident commander and scribe). Doctors first stabilize the patient, stopping the bleeding and getting vitals safe (mitigation), before running full diagnostics and performing the definitive surgery that fixes the underlying condition (resolution). Stabilizing the patient fast is not the same as curing them; both matter, in that order. Afterward the team reviews the case to improve protocols (blameless postmortem).

commonMisconceptions.myth: An incident is only over once you know the root cause.
commonMisconceptions.reality: An incident's consumer impact ends at mitigation; the root cause can be resolved calmly afterward. Restoring trusted data (serving last-known-good, pausing the DAG) is separate from and usually faster than the permanent fix.

commonMisconceptions.myth: If the Airflow DAG succeeded, there is no incident.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Data incidents are frequently silent: the job runs green while the data is wrong, stale, or duplicated. Detection must monitor data SLIs (freshness, volume, quality), not just task status.

commonMisconceptions.myth: The incident commander is the most senior engineer or the one fixing the problem.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The IC is a coordination role focused on decisions and communication, not the hands-on fixer. Often a less-loaded person should be IC so the expert can focus on the actual repair.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Route alerts by dataset ownership and severity so a large data estate does not overwhelm one on-call; drive triage from a centralized lineage graph (OpenLineage) rather than tribal knowledge, and automate common mitigations (auto-pause DAG on quality failure) so humans handle only ambiguous incidents.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Make detection deterministic and mitigation idempotent so a paused DAG, quarantine, or rollback can be safely repeated; version dbt models and pipeline config in Git so rollbacks are one command, and keep last-known-good snapshots so serving-around is always possible.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Quarantine bad partitions instead of dropping them so nothing is lost during response, design pipelines so one bad partition does not corrupt others, and ensure mitigations degrade gracefully (serve stale-but-correct rather than fail hard).
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Track SLIs (freshness lag, volume delta, null rate, distribution drift, schema changes) with baselines and dashboards, and instrument the lifecycle itself with MTTD/MTTA/MTTR/MTTU so the response process is observable, not just the pipelines.
productionConsiderations.security: Restrict who can pause DAGs, roll back models, or repoint production views to authorized on-call responders; keep incident channels and postmortems free of raw PII from failing rows, and audit-log every mitigation action for compliance.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Prefer cheap mitigations (repoint to last-known-good) over expensive full backfills when they suffice, scope backfills to affected partitions rather than reprocessing whole tables, and tune SLIs to cut false pages that waste on-call time.
productionConsiderations.performance: Compute SLIs incrementally on new partitions rather than full-table scans to keep MTTD low, precompute lineage so blast-radius queries return in seconds during triage, and parallelize partition-scoped backfills to shorten MTTU.

codeExamples.title: Incident Automation: detect, page, and open an incident channel
codeExamples.overview: A Python handler that runs when a Great Expectations / freshness check fails, assesses severity from lineage, pages PagerDuty, and opens a Slack incident channel with roles pre-assigned.
codeExamples.breakdown: downstream_impact() calls the OpenLineage/Marquez API to enumerate everything downstream of the broken table, which is the blast radius. severity() maps blast radius to a SEV using a critical-consumer set and a count threshold, so triage is automated and consistent. handle_check_failure() records the detection timestamp (feeding MTTD), triggers a PagerDuty page whose urgency scales with severity, and opens a dedicated Slack incident channel. The returned dict is the seed of the incident record and postmortem timeline.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: {'severity': 'SEV1', 'blast_radius': 12, 'consumers': ['dataset:snowflake:exec_revenue_dashboard', ...], 'detected_at': '2026-07-03T06:05:11'} plus a triggered PagerDuty incident and a new #inc-2026-07-03-orders_reve Slack channel.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Hardcoding routing keys/tokens instead of using a secrets manager; the lineage call timing out during an incident (precompute or cache it); severity logic that ignores freshness-only vs correctness incidents; missing pagination when a table has many downstream consumers.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Cache the lineage graph so blast-radius lookups return in milliseconds during triage; make severity data-driven from a table-criticality catalog rather than a hardcoded set; add deduplication so repeated check failures update the existing incident instead of paging repeatedly.

codeExamples.title: SQL: quantify blast radius and financial impact of a bad load
codeExamples.overview: During triage, quantify how wrong the current partition is versus the last-known-good baseline and how many downstream rows/consumers are affected, to justify severity.
codeExamples.code:
-- 1) How bad is today's load vs the trailing baseline (Snowflake)?
WITH today AS (
  SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_today,
         SUM(amount) AS revenue_today,
         COUNT_IF(amount < 0) AS negative_amounts
  FROM analytics.orders_revenue_mart
  WHERE load_date = CURRENT_DATE
),
baseline AS (
  SELECT AVG(daily_rows) AS avg_rows,
         AVG(daily_revenue) AS avg_revenue
  FROM (
    SELECT load_date,
           COUNT(*) AS daily_rows,
           SUM(amount) AS daily_revenue
    FROM analytics.orders_revenue_mart
    WHERE load_date BETWEEN CURRENT_DATE - 14 AND CURRENT_DATE - 1
    GROUP BY load_date
  )
)
SELECT t.rows_today, b.avg_rows,
       ROUND(t.revenue_today / NULLIF(b.avg_revenue,0), 1) AS revenue_ratio, -- ~100x = smoking gun
       t.negative_amounts
FROM today t CROSS JOIN baseline b;

-- 2) Blast radius: which downstream models/dashboards consume the broken table?
SELECT referencing_object_name AS downstream_object,
       referencing_object_domain AS object_type
FROM snowflake.account_usage.object_dependencies
WHERE referenced_object_name = 'ORDERS_REVENUE_MART'
ORDER BY object_type;
codeExamples.breakdown: The first query compares today's row count and revenue against a 14-day trailing baseline; a revenue_ratio near 100 is the smoking gun for the cents-vs-dollars bug and quantifies exactly how wrong the data is, which drives severity. The second query uses Snowflake's account_usage.object_dependencies (or BigQuery's INFORMATION_SCHEMA equivalent) to enumerate every downstream object that references the broken mart, giving the concrete blast radius list to warn consumers and scope the backfill.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: rows_today=48210, avg_rows=47950, revenue_ratio=99.4, negative_amounts=0 (volume normal but revenue ~100x inflated), and a downstream list such as VW_EXEC_REVENUE (VIEW), PRICING_FEATURES (TABLE), FINANCE_MART (TABLE), plus 9 dbt models.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Comparing against a baseline that already includes the bad day; forgetting timezone when bucketing load_date; account_usage having up to ~90 min latency so dependencies may be slightly stale during a very fresh incident; not distinguishing views (auto-fix on source repair) from materialized tables (need backfill).
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Materialize daily baseline metrics into a small metrics-history table so this comparison is instant; maintain a curated lineage table (from OpenLineage) that is fresher than account_usage; tag downstream objects with criticality so the query returns severity directly.

codeExamples.title: Mitigation and resolution: pause DAG, serve last-known-good, then backfill
codeExamples.overview: A bash/dbt sequence showing the two distinct phases: fast mitigation (pause + repoint to last-known-good), then resolution (patch, partition-scoped backfill, verify SLIs).
codeExamples.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
INC="inc-2026-0142"; PARTITION="2026-07-03"

# ---------- MITIGATE: stop the bleeding ----------
# 1) Pause the offending DAG so no more bad data lands
airflow dags pause orders_daily_load

# 2) Quarantine today's bad partition (do not drop it)
snow sql -q "CREATE TABLE quarantine.orders_${PARTITION//-/} AS \
  SELECT * FROM analytics.orders_revenue_mart WHERE load_date = '${PARTITION}'; \
  DELETE FROM analytics.orders_revenue_mart WHERE load_date = '${PARTITION}';"

# 3) Serve last-known-good: repoint the consumer view to yesterday's validated snapshot
snow sql -q "CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW analytics.vw_exec_revenue AS \
  SELECT * FROM analytics.orders_revenue_mart WHERE load_date < '${PARTITION}';"
echo "[$INC] MITIGATED: DAG paused, partition quarantined, consumers on last-known-good"

# ---------- RESOLVE: permanent fix + recovery ----------
# 4) Deploy the root-cause fix (cents->dollars) already merged to main
git -C /opt/dbt pull --ff-only

# 5) Backfill ONLY the affected partition, then rebuild downstream models
dbt run --select orders_revenue_mart+ --vars "{load_date: ${PARTITION}}" --target prod

# 6) Verify SLIs recovered before restoring live consumers
dbt test --select orders_revenue_mart+ --target prod
snow sql -q "CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW analytics.vw_exec_revenue AS \
  SELECT * FROM analytics.orders_revenue_mart;"   -- point consumers back at live data
airflow dags unpause orders_daily_load
echo "[$INC] RESOLVED: fix deployed, partition backfilled, SLIs green, consumers on live data"
codeExamples.breakdown: The script is deliberately split into two labeled phases. MITIGATE pauses the Airflow DAG (no new bad data), quarantines rather than drops the bad partition (nothing lost, auditable), and repoints the consumer view to the last validated snapshot so the exec dashboard shows correct-but-stale data immediately. RESOLVE pulls the merged fix, runs a partition-scoped dbt backfill (orders_revenue_mart+ rebuilds the model and everything downstream), runs dbt test to confirm quality SLIs pass, and only then repoints consumers to live data and unpauses the DAG. This ordering is the whole point: consumers are protected during the entire resolution.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
[inc-2026-0142] MITIGATED: DAG paused, partition quarantined, consumers on last-known-good
[inc-2026-0142] RESOLVED: fix deployed, partition backfilled, SLIs green, consumers on live data
codeExamples.commonIssues: Unpausing the DAG before the fix is deployed (re-lands bad data); dropping instead of quarantining the partition (unrecoverable); backfilling the whole table instead of the affected partition (slow, costly); repointing to live data before dbt test passes (re-exposes consumers to bad data).
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Wrap the mitigation block in a self-service runbook or an incident-bot slash command so any on-call can execute it safely; parameterize partition and DAG names; add an automatic reconciliation check (mart total vs source total) as the final gate before restoring live consumers.

codeExamples.title: Alerting rule: freshness and volume SLIs (Prometheus/Alertmanager YAML)
codeExamples.overview: Declarative alert rules that detect the two most common data incidents (stale data and volume anomalies) and route them to PagerDuty with severity labels.
codeExamples.code:
groups:
  - name: data_reliability_slis
    rules:
      # DETECT: freshness SLI - table not updated within SLA window
      - alert: TableStale
        expr: |
          (time() - data_table_last_success_timestamp_seconds{table="orders_revenue_mart"}) > 3600
        for: 5m
        labels:
          severity: sev2
          team: data-platform
          service: pagerduty
        annotations:
          summary: "orders_revenue_mart is stale (>1h past SLA)"
          runbook: "https://runbooks/data/freshness"
          mitigation: "Check upstream Airflow DAG; if source down, serve last-known-good"

      # DETECT: volume anomaly - row count deviates >40% from 14d baseline
      - alert: VolumeAnomaly
        expr: |
          abs(
            data_table_row_count{table="orders_revenue_mart"}
            - data_table_row_count_baseline_14d{table="orders_revenue_mart"}
          ) / data_table_row_count_baseline_14d{table="orders_revenue_mart"} > 0.40
        for: 0m
        labels:
          severity: sev1
          team: data-platform
          service: pagerduty
        annotations:
          summary: "orders_revenue_mart row count off >40% from baseline"
          runbook: "https://runbooks/data/volume"
          mitigation: "Quarantine partition; pause DAG; assess blast radius via lineage"
codeExamples.breakdown: Each rule is an SLI made executable. TableStale computes freshness as now minus the last successful load timestamp and fires when it exceeds the 1-hour SLA sustained for 5 minutes (the for clause suppresses flapping). VolumeAnomaly compares the current row count to a precomputed 14-day baseline metric and fires immediately on a >40% deviation. Labels drive routing and severity in Alertmanager (to PagerDuty), and annotations embed the runbook link and the first mitigation step so the on-call starts triage with context instead of a blank page.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: When orders_revenue_mart's row count deviates >40%, Alertmanager routes a SEV1 to PagerDuty within seconds with summary 'orders_revenue_mart row count off >40% from baseline' and the embedded mitigation hint; a stale table fires SEV2 after 5 minutes past SLA.
codeExamples.commonIssues: No 'for' clause causing flappy freshness pages; static thresholds that ignore seasonality (weekend volume dips); baseline metric that silently includes bad days; alert lacking a runbook so the on-call wastes minutes finding context.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Use a rolling/seasonal baseline (day-of-week aware) to cut false positives; add inhibition rules so a known source outage suppresses downstream alerts; include the owning team and the first mitigation step in every annotation to shorten MTTA.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A subscription commerce company reports daily revenue to the executive team at 08:00 and feeds a pricing ML model from the same tables. An upstream billing API change silently switched the amount field from dollars to cents, so the revenue mart shows numbers ~100x too high while every Airflow task still succeeds. The company needs a fast, structured response that stops executives and the pricing model from consuming wrong data, restores trusted numbers before the 08:00 deck, and prevents recurrence.
endToEndExample.inputData: Kafka-streamed billing events ingested by an Airflow DAG (orders_daily_load) into Snowflake, transformed by dbt into analytics.orders_revenue_mart. Each event has transaction_id, user_id, amount, currency, and event_timestamp. Downstream: exec revenue dashboard view, 11 dbt models, and a pricing_features table.
endToEndExample.architecture: Kafka -> Airflow ingest DAG -> dbt transforms -> Snowflake analytics layer -> Great Expectations quality checkpoint + Prometheus freshness/volume SLIs -> Alertmanager -> PagerDuty on-call. OpenLineage/Marquez provides lineage for triage. An incident bot manages Slack channels and roles; a quarantine schema and last-known-good snapshots support mitigation.
processingSteps: 1. DETECT: At 06:05 a Great Expectations distribution check on orders_revenue_mart fails (revenue p99 ~100x baseline) while freshness/volume stay green; the failure pages the data on-call via PagerDuty. MTTD = 15 min.

2. TRIAGE: The on-call acks at 06:12 (MTTA = 7 min), runs the blast-radius SQL and OpenLineage query, and finds the exec dashboard, pricing_features, and 11 dbt models affected. Severity is set to SEV1 because of the 08:00 board deck and the pricing model dependency.

3. DECLARE: An incident is declared: #inc-2026-0142 opens automatically, an incident commander, comms lead, and scribe are assigned, and the comms lead posts a stakeholder message that revenue data is degraded with an ETA.

4. MITIGATE: The team pauses orders_daily_load, quarantines today's partition, and repoints the exec view to yesterday's validated snapshot (last-known-good). Consumers now see correct-but-stale data. Service restored at 06:40. MTTR = 35 min.

5. RESOLVE: Engineers patch the dbt model (divide the miscoded field by 100 and add a validity check), run a partition-scoped dbt backfill (orders_revenue_mart+), and re-run the 11 downstream models plus pricing_features.

6. VERIFY & CLOSE: dbt test passes, a reconciliation check confirms the mart total matches source, freshness catches up, and the exec view is repointed to live data. The incident is closed at 07:30 (MTTU = 85 min) and a blameless postmortem is scheduled.

7. LEARN: The postmortem captures the timeline from the scribe's log, identifies the missing source-schema contract as the contributing factor, and files action items (schema contract test, currency validity check, seasonality-aware volume alert).
endToEndExample.output: Correct revenue data delivered before the 08:00 board deck; the pricing model retrained on validated features; a quarantined partition preserved for audit; a full incident timeline; and a scheduled blameless postmortem with tracked action items.
endToEndExample.monitoring: Grafana dashboards show freshness lag, row-count vs baseline, null rate, and distribution drift per table; a separate reliability dashboard tracks MTTD, MTTA, MTTR, and MTTU per incident and SLO/error-budget burn for the revenue data product.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: Detection fails-loud via GE + Prometheus; the bad partition is quarantined not dropped; the DAG is paused to stop re-landing bad data; consumers are served last-known-good during resolution; and the live view is only restored after dbt test and reconciliation pass, so consumers are never re-exposed to bad data.
endToEndExample.finalResult: Executives received correct numbers on time, the pricing model was protected from corrupted features, and time-to-detection dropped from 'a stakeholder noticing next day' to 15 minutes because content SLIs replaced job-only monitoring. The postmortem's schema-contract action item eliminated the entire class of silent currency bugs going forward.

industryUseCases.problem: Thousands of data pipelines feed personalization, forecasting, and finance, and silent data issues could corrupt models and reports before anyone noticed, making manual detection and triage impossible at scale.
industryUseCases.solution: Netflix built data-quality and anomaly-detection tooling (in the WAP write-audit-publish pattern and lineage-aware platforms) that audits data before publishing and pages owners on anomalies, with clear ownership and runbooks for response.
industryUseCases.benefits: Bad data is caught in the audit stage before it reaches consumers, blast radius is scoped via lineage, and incidents are routed to the owning team, cutting time-to-detection and preventing corrupted data from reaching production models.

industryUseCases.problem: Customer data teams learned about incidents only when a stakeholder complained about a broken dashboard, resulting in long, costly 'data downtime' with no structured response.
industryUseCases.solution: A data observability platform that monitors freshness, volume, schema, and distribution, learns baselines, detects anomalies, computes lineage-based blast radius, and integrates with PagerDuty/Slack to drive incident response.
industryUseCases.benefits: Automatic detection with lineage-aware root-cause and impact analysis sharply reduces MTTD and MTTR, letting teams mitigate (notify consumers, pause pipelines) before wrong data propagates widely.

industryUseCases.problem: With thousands of derived datasets, engineers could not quickly tell which tables were trustworthy or what an incident's downstream impact was, slowing triage.
industryUseCases.solution: Airbnb built data lineage, dataset certification, and quality scoring (Dataportal and related tooling) so ownership, trust signals, and downstream dependencies are visible and searchable during an incident.
industryUseCases.benefits: Responders quickly identify blast radius and owners, right-size severity, and communicate to the correct downstream consumers, turning triage from tribal guesswork into a lineage-driven step.

industryUseCases.problem: Operational and analytical data pipelines are business-critical (pricing, ETA, finance), so undetected data incidents directly harm the marketplace and require an SRE-grade response.
industryUseCases.solution: Uber applies SRE practices to data: SLOs on data products, on-call rotations, quality checks, and lineage in its data platform, with structured incident management and postmortems adapted from service reliability.
industryUseCases.benefits: Data incidents are detected, triaged with severity and lineage, mitigated fast, and reviewed blamelessly, keeping critical marketplace data reliable at massive scale.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Route alerts by dataset ownership so a large estate does not funnel every page to one on-call; drive triage from a centralized OpenLineage graph rather than tribal knowledge; automate high-confidence mitigations (auto-pause a DAG on a hard quality failure) so humans are reserved for ambiguous SEV1/SEV2s; and precompute blast-radius so lineage lookups stay fast as dependency counts grow.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Quarantine bad partitions instead of dropping them so nothing is lost during response; partition pipelines so one corrupt partition cannot poison others; make every mitigation idempotent (pausing an already-paused DAG or re-running a quarantine is safe); and always keep a last-known-good snapshot so serving-around is possible even when the source is down.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Run detection and alerting on redundant infrastructure separate from the pipelines they watch (a monitoring outage must not blind you); maintain primary/secondary on-call in PagerDuty with escalation policies; and serve last-known-good data so a data product stays available (if stale) to consumers throughout an incident.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Keep versioned dbt models and pipeline config in Git so rollback is a single revert; retain quarantined partitions and source data so any affected window can be reprocessed; snapshot warehouse tables (Snowflake Time Travel / BigQuery snapshots) so you can restore a table to a pre-incident state; and store metrics history so you can prove what 'good' looked like before the incident.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Compute SLIs incrementally on new partitions to keep MTTD low; cache the lineage graph so blast-radius queries return in seconds during triage; scope backfills to affected partitions and parallelize them to shorten MTTU; and precompute baseline metrics into a small history table so triage comparisons are instant.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Prefer cheap mitigations (repoint to last-known-good, pause DAG) over expensive full-table backfills when they suffice; scope reprocessing to affected partitions; tune SLIs to eliminate false pages that waste on-call hours; and use approximate metrics for cheap frequent checks, reserving exact heavy checks for critical products.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Restrict who can pause DAGs, roll back models, or repoint production views to authorized responders via RBAC; keep incident channels, alerts, and postmortems free of raw PII from failing rows (log row keys, not values); audit-log every mitigation action; and ensure quarantine tables inherit the same access controls and retention limits as the source.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Monitor data SLIs (freshness, volume, null rate, distribution, schema) with baselines and anomaly detection layered on top of job monitoring; expose per-table dashboards in Grafana; and instrument the lifecycle itself with MTTD/MTTA/MTTR/MTTU and error-budget burn so the response process, not just the pipelines, is observable and improvable.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Gate publication with quality checks (Great Expectations/dbt tests) so many incidents are prevented at the boundary; during resolution, re-run those checks plus a reconciliation of the fixed mart against source before restoring live consumers; and treat a passed quality suite plus caught-up freshness as the objective definition of 'SLIs recovered' that closes the incident.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Route alerts to the owning team with severity labels, a runbook link, and the first mitigation step embedded so triage starts with context; use 'for' clauses and inhibition rules to suppress flapping and downstream noise during a known outage; deduplicate repeated failures into one incident; and have the scribe (or the incident bot) log every action with timestamps to build the postmortem timeline automatically.

recommendedPractices: **Mitigate before you resolve:** always take the fastest safe action to protect consumers (pause DAG, serve last-known-good) before hunting the root cause.
**Monitor data content, not just jobs:** layer freshness, volume, and quality SLIs on top of task-success monitoring so silent corruption is detected.
**Drive triage from lineage:** compute blast radius via OpenLineage/dbt DAG to set true severity and warn the right consumers.
**Assign roles at declaration:** name an incident commander, comms lead, and scribe so fixing, communicating, and documenting happen in parallel.
**Quarantine, never drop:** preserve bad partitions for audit and reprocessing rather than deleting them during response.
**Verify SLIs before closing:** confirm quality checks pass, freshness caught up, and the mart reconciles to source before declaring resolution.
engineeringStandards: Every critical data product has a named owner, an SLO (freshness and correctness), and an on-call rotation in PagerDuty/Opsgenie.
Severity levels (SEV1-SEV4) are documented with objective criteria and required communication cadence for each.
dbt models and pipeline config live in version control so rollback is a single, auditable command.
Mitigation actions (pause, quarantine, rollback, repoint) are codified as runbooks or incident-bot commands, not improvised.
Every SEV1/SEV2 produces a blameless postmortem with tracked, owned action items.
designRecommendations: Design pipelines with write-audit-publish so bad data is caught before consumers ever see it.
Keep last-known-good snapshots and consumer-facing views decoupled from underlying tables so repointing is instant.
Partition data so incidents and backfills are scoped to a single partition rather than whole tables.
Precompute and cache lineage and baseline metrics so triage is fast under pressure.
Automate high-confidence mitigations (auto-pause DAG on hard quality failure) and reserve humans for ambiguity.
namingConventions: Name incident channels consistently, for example inc-YYYY-NNNN or #inc-<date>-<system>.
Name quarantine tables predictably, for example quarantine.<table>_<partition> or <table>_dq_failures.
Name SLI alerts by table and dimension, for example orders_revenue_mart__freshness or __volume_anomaly.
Name last-known-good snapshots clearly, for example <table>_lkg or <table>_snapshot_<date>.
Name severity and roles consistently across tooling (SEV1-SEV4; IC, comms, scribe) so everyone shares vocabulary.
documentationStandards: Maintain a runbook per common incident type (stale table, volume drop, schema change, bad load) with concrete mitigation steps.
Document each data product's SLO, owner, and downstream consumers in a catalog visible during triage.
Record every incident's timeline, severity, MTTD/MTTA/MTTR/MTTU, and action items in a postmortem template.
Keep a severity matrix mapping impact and scope to SEV level and required communication cadence.
Document the mitigation-vs-resolution distinction and the definition of 'SLIs recovered' that closes an incident.
testingStrategies: Run game days / fault injection: deliberately land a bad partition or stale table and verify detection pages and runbooks work.
Test quality gates in CI against sample data so schema/currency regressions are caught before deploy.
Rehearse the incident bridge and role assignments so responders are practiced before a real SEV1.
Backtest SLI thresholds against historical incidents to tune sensitivity and cut false pages.
Verify backfill and rollback runbooks in staging so the resolution path is proven before it is needed in production.

commonMistakes.mistake: Chasing root cause before mitigating, leaving bad data live the whole time.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Engineers instinctively want to understand and fix the problem, and mitigation feels like a hack rather than 'real' work.
commonMistakes.impact: Consumers keep ingesting wrong data for the entire investigation, multiplying the blast radius and business damage.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Restore trust first (pause DAG, quarantine, serve last-known-good), then diagnose and resolve the root cause calmly with consumers already protected.

commonMistakes.mistake: Only paging on job/task failures, so silent data corruption is never detected.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Orchestrators expose task status out of the box, while data-content SLIs require deliberate instrumentation.
commonMistakes.impact: Green pipelines ship wrong, stale, or duplicated data undetected until a stakeholder complains, blowing up MTTD.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Instrument freshness, volume, null rate, distribution, and schema SLIs with baselines and page on those, not just on task failures.

commonMistakes.mistake: Setting severity from the broken table's importance instead of its blast radius.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Without lineage, responders judge severity by what they can see, not by what depends on it.
commonMistakes.impact: A small staging table feeding the board deck is under-triaged, or a trivial dead-end table triggers a needless SEV1.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Compute blast radius via lineage and set severity from downstream consumer impact, not the table itself.

commonMistakes.mistake: Dropping the bad partition to 'clean up' instead of quarantining it.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Deleting the offending rows feels like the quickest way to make the numbers look right again.
commonMistakes.impact: The data needed to diagnose and reprocess is lost, and there is no audit trail of what was rejected or why.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Quarantine the partition to a dedicated table, then reprocess it after the fix; never destroy evidence during an incident.

commonMistakes.mistake: Declaring the incident resolved at mitigation and skipping verification.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Once consumers stop complaining, the pressure drops and the team moves on before confirming full recovery.
commonMistakes.impact: Backfills are incomplete or the fix is wrong, so the incident silently recurs or downstream models stay corrupted.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Only close after SLIs are verified (quality checks pass, freshness caught up, mart reconciles to source) and hand off to a blameless postmortem.

comparisonSection.explanation: Mitigation is the fast action that restores trusted service to consumers (pause DAG, serve last-known-good) and ends consumer impact. Resolution is the slower permanent fix (patch code, backfill, verify) that ends the incident. Mitigation comes first; confusing the two leaves consumers exposed while you debug.

Job monitoring answers 'did the DAG run?' and catches crashes and timeouts. Data SLI monitoring answers 'is the data correct, fresh, and complete?' and catches silent corruption in green pipelines. Data incidents frequently occur with all jobs green, so SLI monitoring is essential, not optional.

Quarantining preserves the bad data for diagnosis, reprocessing, and audit while removing it from consumer-facing tables. Dropping makes the numbers look right immediately but destroys the evidence needed to fix and backfill, so quarantine is almost always correct.

Severity should follow who is impacted, discovered via lineage, not the intuitive importance of the table. A modest table feeding the board deck is high severity; a 'big' table with no live consumers is low. Lineage-driven severity right-sizes the response.

The IC coordinates, decides, and keeps communication flowing but does not typically do the repair; the fixer focuses on the technical fix. Combining both in one person under stress slows both. Separating them lets the expert fix while the IC drives the process.

beginnerQuestions.question: What are the four phases of the incident response lifecycle?
beginnerQuestions.answer: Detect (recognize the problem, ideally automatically via SLIs), triage (assess severity and blast radius, declare the incident, assign roles), mitigate (stop the bleeding and restore trusted data fast), and resolve (fix the root cause, backfill, verify SLIs recovered, close, and hand off to a postmortem).
beginnerQuestions.explanation: A strong answer names all four in order and shows they can overlap, and ideally notes that mitigation and resolution are distinct steps.

beginnerQuestions.question: In data engineering, why isn't a successful pipeline run enough to say there's no incident?
beginnerQuestions.answer: Because data incidents are often silent: the DAG runs green while the data is wrong, stale, or duplicated. Orchestrators report whether the code ran, not whether the output is correct, so you must monitor data SLIs like freshness, volume, and quality to detect these incidents.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Interviewers want to hear that job success and data correctness are independent and that detection must cover data content.

intermediateQuestions.question: How do mitigation and resolution differ, and why does the distinction matter?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Mitigation is the fast action that restores trusted service to consumers without necessarily fixing the cause, such as pausing the DAG, quarantining the bad partition, rolling back a dbt model, or serving last-known-good. Resolution is the permanent fix plus reprocessing and verification. The distinction matters because you want to stop consumer harm in minutes even though root-cause fixing may take hours; mitigating first shrinks blast radius while you resolve calmly.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: A good answer gives concrete data-specific mitigations and stresses that mitigation ends consumer impact while resolution ends the incident.

intermediateQuestions.question: How would you determine the severity of a data incident?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Severity is a function of impact and scope. Compute blast radius via lineage (OpenLineage, dbt DAG, or warehouse dependency graph) to find all downstream consumers, then classify by who is affected (board deck, customer-facing metric, ML feature) and how many products. A small table feeding the exec dashboard is SEV1; a large table with no live consumers may be SEV3. Time-sensitivity (an 08:00 deck) also raises severity.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Interviewers look for lineage-driven, impact-based severity rather than judging the table in isolation.

advancedQuestions.question: Design an on-call and incident process for a platform with hundreds of data products.
advancedQuestions.answer: Assign each data product an owner, an SLO, and a PagerDuty rotation; route alerts by ownership and severity. Instrument data SLIs (freshness, volume, quality, schema) with baselines feeding Alertmanager. Drive triage from a centralized lineage graph so blast radius and severity are computed automatically. Codify mitigations as runbooks/incident-bot commands and automate high-confidence ones. Track MTTD/MTTA/MTTR/MTTU and error-budget burn, and require blameless postmortems with owned action items for SEV1/SEV2.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Strong answers scale via ownership, centralized lineage, automation, and lifecycle metrics rather than bespoke per-table handling.

advancedQuestions.question: How do you measure whether your incident response is actually improving?
advancedQuestions.answer: Instrument the lifecycle with MTTD (detect), MTTA (acknowledge), MTTR (restore/mitigate), and MTTU (ultimately resolve), tracked per incident and trended over time, plus incident count by severity and error-budget burn per data product. Falling MTTD means detection is improving; falling MTTA means on-call is responsive; falling MTTR means mitigation runbooks work; falling MTTU means resolution/backfill is faster. Postmortem action-item completion rate shows whether learning is closing the loop.
advancedQuestions.explanation: The interviewer wants the four metrics tied to specific parts of the lifecycle and the postmortem feedback loop.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: At 06:05 a quality check flags that the revenue mart is ~100x too high, but every Airflow task is green. The board deck is due at 08:00. What do you do?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: First establish blast radius via lineage and set severity (board deck + any ML consumers likely SEV1). The immediate goal is to protect consumers before the deck, so mitigate before diagnosing. A 100x factor screams a units bug (cents vs dollars). Mitigate by pausing the DAG, quarantining the partition, and serving last-known-good; then resolve by patching the model, backfilling the partition, verifying, and reconciling before restoring live data.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Declare a SEV1 and assign IC/comms/scribe. Query lineage to enumerate downstream consumers and warn them. Mitigate immediately: pause the orders DAG so no more bad data lands, quarantine today's partition (do not drop it), and repoint the exec view to yesterday's validated snapshot so the deck can use correct-but-stale numbers if needed. Then resolve: confirm the cents-vs-dollars root cause, patch the dbt model and add a currency validity check, run a partition-scoped backfill, re-run downstream models, and only repoint to live data after dbt test passes and the mart reconciles to source. Close and run a blameless postmortem with a schema-contract action item.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: Your data on-call is being paged 15 times a night, mostly false alarms, and real incidents are being missed. How do you fix it?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: This is alert fatigue harming MTTD. Investigate which alerts fire most and whether they map to real consumer impact. Likely causes: static thresholds ignoring seasonality, no 'for' clause causing flapping, no inhibition so one source outage fans out into many downstream pages, and non-actionable alerts. Fix by tuning, deduplicating, inhibiting, and routing by ownership.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Audit alert volume vs true positives, then tune: add 'for' clauses to stop flapping, use seasonality/day-of-week-aware baselines instead of static thresholds, add inhibition rules so an upstream outage suppresses downstream pages, deduplicate repeated failures into one incident, and delete non-actionable alerts. Route by dataset ownership so each on-call only gets their pages, attach runbooks so every page is actionable, and track false-positive rate as a metric. The goal is fewer, higher-signal pages so real incidents surface and MTTD improves.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design an incident response system for a data platform where wrong data currently reaches executives before anyone notices.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Add a detection layer of data SLIs (freshness, volume, null rate, distribution, schema) computed incrementally per load and evaluated against seasonal baselines, feeding Alertmanager -> PagerDuty. On alert, an automation looks up blast radius from OpenLineage, sets severity, pages the owner, and opens a Slack incident channel with roles. Provide codified mitigations (pause DAG, quarantine partition, rollback dbt model, serve last-known-good) as incident-bot commands, and a resolution path (patch, partition-scoped backfill, verify SLIs, reconcile). Instrument MTTD/MTTA/MTTR/MTTU and require blameless postmortems.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: More SLIs and automation improve detection and speed but add maintenance and alert-fatigue risk, so tier rigor by data-product criticality. Auto-mitigation is fast but risky for ambiguous cases, so restrict it to high-confidence hard failures. Serving last-known-good keeps availability but exposes staleness, which must be clearly labeled to consumers.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Route by ownership so the process scales across hundreds of products; centralize and cache lineage so triage stays fast; compute SLIs incrementally and precompute baselines to keep MTTD low; scope backfills to partitions; and standardize severity, roles, and runbooks so any on-call can respond without bespoke knowledge.

followUpQuestions: What is the difference between MTTR and MTTU, and why track both?
How does lineage change your triage and severity decisions?
What are concrete data-specific mitigations that don't fix the root cause?
Why should the incident commander usually not be the person fixing the problem?
What makes a postmortem 'blameless' and why does that matter?
When would you serve last-known-good versus backfill immediately?

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: The incident response lifecycle is the structured process for data-reliability incidents across four phases (detect, triage, mitigate, resolve), with defined severity and roles, that restores trusted data fast then fixes the root cause, measured by MTTD/MTTA/MTTR/MTTU.
keyConcepts: Four phases: detect -> triage -> mitigate -> resolve.
Mitigation restores trusted service fast; resolution is the permanent root-cause fix.
Green jobs can still be incidents; monitor data SLIs, not just task status.
Severity comes from lineage-based blast radius, not the broken table's importance.
Roles: incident commander (coordinates), comms lead (updates), scribe (timeline).
Quarantine bad partitions; never drop them during response.
Close only after SLIs are verified recovered; hand off to a blameless postmortem.
formulas: Blast radius = count(downstream consumers via lineage)
Error budget burn = 1 - (good_windows / total_windows) vs SLO target
commands: Airflow: airflow dags pause <dag> ; airflow dags unpause <dag>
dbt backfill: dbt run --select model+ --vars '{load_date: YYYY-MM-DD}' ; dbt test --select model+
Snowflake LKG view: CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW vw AS SELECT * FROM tbl WHERE load_date < '<bad_date>';
Blast radius: SELECT referencing_object_name FROM snowflake.account_usage.object_dependencies WHERE referenced_object_name='TBL';
interviewPoints: Name the four phases and their order.
Distinguish mitigation (fast service restore) from resolution (permanent fix).
Detection must cover data content, not just job success.
Set severity from lineage-based blast radius.
Quarantine, don't drop; verify SLIs before closing; run a blameless postmortem.
quickNotes: Serve last-known-good to keep consumers safe during resolution.
IC coordinates; expert fixes; scribe logs the timeline.
Track MTTD/MTTA/MTTR/MTTU to know what to improve.
Tune alerts (for-clauses, seasonality, inhibition) to beat alert fatigue.

keyTakeaways: The incident response lifecycle has four phases: detect, triage, mitigate, resolve, with clear severity levels and roles (incident commander, comms lead, scribe) that make firefighting predictable.
In data engineering, incidents are often silent (green jobs, wrong data), so detection must monitor data SLIs such as freshness, volume, and quality, not just task success.

Mitigation and resolution are distinct: mitigation (pause DAG, quarantine partition, roll back a dbt model, serve last-known-good) restores trusted service fast, while resolution fixes the root cause and backfills; always mitigate first.
Triage severity from lineage-based blast radius, not the broken table's own importance, so the response is right-sized and the correct consumers are warned.

Close an incident only after verifying SLIs have recovered (quality checks pass, freshness caught up, mart reconciles to source), then hand off to a blameless postmortem and track MTTD/MTTA/MTTR/MTTU to improve.
